title: A hymn that ends on perhaps
hookLine: the summit sit, looking back over a year that kept asking questions, from a king in a forest to a hymn that wonders who really knows
carry: in hinduism, asking is part of the path

cards: The hymn of creation in the Rig Veda asks it near its end, and then, in paraphrase, says this about the one who watches over everything from the highest heaven: perhaps he knows, or perhaps he does not know.
That hymn stands in the scripture, question and all. And from the top of year four, it doesn't sit alone. This whole year kept stopping at questions.
Today, the year close, told by the questions it asked.

teach.b: It opened with one. A king who'd lost his kingdom and a merchant thrown out by his family asked a sage: we know these things have left us, so why doesn't knowing help? The whole Devi Mahatmya is the answer.

Then the questions got sharper. The schools of thought asked how anyone knows anything at all, and the path let each answer in its own way. The Vedas asked in their own voice: what covered it, where, in whose keeping?
Then came the women, several of them remembered for a question.
Gargi asked Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, and when he told her to stop, she came back with two more. Maitreyi asked what she'd do with wealth that can't make her immortal.
There's a name for this in the tradition.
The Brahma Sutra, a founding text of Vedanta, opens with one short line: athato brahma jijnasa. Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman, the longing to know the ultimate. Not a creed to sign first.
A question to ask. That's the big teaching under year four.
In Hinduism, honest asking isn't a lapse in faith. It's one of the doors in. A tradition could have kept only the answers.
This one kept the questions inside its sacred texts, and some are never closed.
The hymn of creation ends on perhaps.

So that's year four from the top: the goddess, Shiva, the schools, the Vedas, the women and the regions, and running through all of them, people asking out loud, and a tradition that kept their questions.

how: Hindu traditions keep questions inside their texts: the Upanishads hold dialogues between teachers and questioners, the Brahma Sutra opens with inquiry, and the hymn of creation, with its open last line, is chanted as part of the Rig Veda.

o: the fourth year, looked back on by the questions it asked
a fourth exam that tests everything learned so far
the fourth year, judged by the answers it settled

games.q: the questions of year four — tap the pairs.
p: on what is the world woven?

s: the hymn of creation ends with a confident answer
it ends on perhaps: perhaps he knows, or perhaps he does not know.
Gargi stops asking for good once Yajnavalkya warns her
she comes back later with two more questions.
this year let each school of thought answer in its own way
the schools were taught side by side, and none was ranked.

games.q: you're compiling a sacred collection. one hymn about creation ends by wondering whether even the one in the highest heaven knows. what do you do with it?
o: keep it, and chant it with the rest.
games.why: the hymn was kept in the Rig Veda, open last line and all, and is still chanted.

practice: Let one real question rise, something you don't know the answer to, about your life, or about God, or about anything, and let it sit beside you the way the hymn lets its last line sit.
Each time the mind starts building an answer, come back to the breath, and to the question, still open. If you pray, you can hold it before God, or the goddess, as it is.

wordCard.voice: Year four. The goddess, Shiva, the schools of thought, the Vedas, the women and the regions, looked at from the top by the questions they asked. Today's word.

orig.note: Vedic Sanskrit: ko addhā veda, who really knows? from the hymn of creation, Rig Veda 10.129.

carryVoice: Your line: in Hinduism, asking is part of the path. Tomorrow, the last day of the year. I'll be here tomorrow.
